item.research_question: What is the intrinsic lattice response of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to external stimuli when pre-existing defects like dislocations are minimized, and does this lead to a new form of elastic instability?
item.material_system: Nanoscale BCC-structured high-entropy alloys: TiHfZrNb (quaternary), TiHfZrNbTa (quinary), TiZrNb (ternary), and binary ZrNb; compared with elemental Nb and FCC HEAs (FeCoNiCrCu, FeCoNiCrMn)
item.processing_route: Alloys prepared by vacuum arc melting (8+ remelts); nanoscale dog-bone samples synthesized via in situ welding in TEM using square electric pulses (1 ms duration, 0-2 V voltage); samples stretched quasi-statically at a strain rate of ∽10⁻³ s⁻¹
item.test_conditions: In situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) under uniaxial tensile loading along [001] and <110> directions; temperature 300 K; electron beam effects verified as negligible
key_findings: Nanoscale BCC HEAs (ternary, quaternary, quinary) undergo elastic strain-induced amorphization at a critical elastic strain of ∽10% without dislocation generation.
The initial BCC lattice elongates into a low-symmetry body-centered tetragonal (BCT) structure before amorphization, with ∽10% elongation along the loading axis and ∽3% lateral contraction.
Binary ZrNb and elemental Nb samples do not exhibit amorphization; instead, they undergo dislocation slip or phase transformation (BCC to FCC) at a lower critical strain of ∽4%.
FCC-structured HEAs (FeCoNiCrCu, FeCoNiCrMn) show dislocation-mediated elastic instability rather than amorphization.
The transition from crystalline to amorphous structure involves a diffusive interface with a transition layer of ∽1.5 nm containing a highly distorted lattice.
Atomic-resolution EDX mapping reveals incipient concentration waves with clustering length scales of ∽2–3 nm in ternary TiZrNb, indicating strong local chemical inhomogeneity.
First-principles and MD simulations confirm that local atomic environment inhomogeneity raises the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation, allowing large elastic strains to accumulate.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the phenomenon to the severe local atomic environment inhomogeneity in HEAs caused by multiple principal elements. This inhomogeneity creates 'hot spots' with varying local atomic displacements, which dramatically reduces the effective volume for dislocation nucleation (N). Consequently, the critical elastic shear strain for dislocation nucleation is significantly increased, preventing premature plastic relaxation. This allows the lattice to sustain elastic strains up to ∽10%, at which point the elastic strain energy overcomes the energy barrier between the crystalline and amorphous structures, triggering instantaneous amorphization.
item.limitations: The lack of in situ tensile curves limits the understanding of the role of mechanical-driven amorphization in the macroscopic mechanical response of nanoscale alloys; the study is restricted to nanoscale samples where defect nucleation is suppressed, so the phenomenon cannot be observed in bulk samples due to premature dislocation generation.
item.future_work: Future work should prioritize integrating capabilities of 0.1 nm precision in displacement loading and nano-newton level force measurement accuracy into in situ TEM mechanical stages to obtain tensile curves.
quotes: Under tensile loading, the HEA lattices are observed to undergo a sudden loss of ordering as the elastic strain reached ∽ 10%.
